name: Appearance and Lighting Decomposition
text:
# Appearance and Lighting Decomposition

Also called: Radiance Decomposition, Material-Lighting Separation

## Overview
Appearance and Lighting Decomposition refers to a family of [neural radiance field (NeRF)](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) architectures that explicitly separate scene properties into geometric, material, and lighting components, rather than predicting raw outgoing radiance as a monolithic function. This [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) solves the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in standard NeRFs and enables downstream tasks such as relighting, material editing, and realistic specular reflection modeling. Unlike standard NeRFs which map position and view direction directly to color, this family reparameterizes the input space (e.g., using surface normals or [spherical harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md)) and outputs distinct physical quantities (e.g., diffuse/specular albedo, roughness, or SH coefficients) that are composed via physically-inspired equations during rendering.

## Shared principles
The core mechanism remains the parametric function $F_\Theta$ that maps a 3D position $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and a viewing direction $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to a volume density $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$ and an RGB color $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3$. This function is implemented as one or more neural networks, typically utilizing [positional encoding](#876-positional-encoding.md) $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ to map raw coordinates to a higher-dimensional space using sinusoidal functions at increasing frequencies [Parent].

**Rendering Integration:**
During training, rays are sampled at points $\mathbf{x}_i$ along the ray. The networks predict $\sigma_i$ and $\mathbf{c}_i$. The pixel color $C(\mathbf{r})$ is computed via volumetric rendering:
$$
C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i \alpha_i \mathbf{c}_i, \quad \text{where } \alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i), \quad T_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)
$$
and $\delta_i$ is the distance between samples [Parent].

**Input Representation:**
Raw coordinates are rarely used directly. They are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$. For a coordinate $\mathbf{x}$, the encoding includes the original value and sinusoidal functions at increasing frequencies:
$$
\gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}))
$$
where $L$ is the number of frequency bands [Parent].

## Subtopics

This family is characterized by how the view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}$ is derived from intermediate scene properties.

### [Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning](9475-anisotropic-neural-representation-learning.md)
[Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning](#9475-anisotropic-neural-representation-learning.md) models volumetric density and latent features as view-dependent functions using spherical harmonics (SH) to eliminate directional ambiguity in neural rendering, replacing the isotropic point-sampled features of [standard NeRF](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) [9475-anisotropic-neural-representation-learning]. Unlike [Mip-NeRF](#3381-mip-nerf.md) which samples cones to approximate pre-filtered representations, this method modifies the MLP to predict view-dependent SH coefficients directly, avoiding the need for shape-based sampling parameterization [9475-anisotropic-neural-representation-learning]. It is designed to be a plug-and-play sub-model that can replace the first MLP in various NeRF-based frameworks to alleviate ambiguity and improve rendering quality [9475-anisotropic-neural-representation-learning].

### [Ref-NeRF](10843-ref-nerf.md)
[Ref-NeRF](#10843-ref-nerf.md) replaces [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)’s parameterization of view-dependent outgoing radiance with a representation of reflected radiance, structured using spatially-varying scene properties to improve specular reflection realism [10843-ref-nerf]. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF and its sibling Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning by explicitly decomposing radiance into diffuse and specular components and reparameterizing the directional input using surface normals, allowing for accurate interpolation of glossy appearances [10843-ref-nerf].

### DE-NeRF
DE-NeRF decomposes lighting, geometry, and appearance to allow relighting of high-frequency environments and appearance editing [S1]. It trains a signed distance field ([SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md)) function using a set of 2D images to reconstruct a display grid as the input scene for the MLP [S1]. The scene is decomposed into geometric features and appearance features ([diffuse reflection](#4896-whitted-style-shading-with-diffuse-glossy-materials.md), roughness, specular tint). Geometric features, appearance features, and distance $h$ (from sampling point to grid) are input into four corresponding MLPs to predict diffuse albedo, roughness value, and specular tint [S1]. Diffuse reflectance is integrated with the environment map to get diffuse color $c_d$. A specular lighting MLP $F_s$ is trained to get specular lighting $c_l$, which is multiplied with specular hue to get specular color $c_s$. The final color is $c = c_s + c_d$ [S1]. On NeRF Synthetic and Shiny Blender data sets, PSNR is 2 points higher than latest papers [S1].

### NeRFLight
NeRFLight extends grid-based methods by dividing the scene into eight different regions to split NeRF into separate density and color fields, using a shared feature grid [S1]. It avoids increasing the number of features for seamless reconstruction while reducing stored feature values [S1]. The scene is divided into eight different regions, each corresponding to an MLP that outputs density and color [S1]. A shared feature grid is used, allowing features to be symmetrically placed at the center of the scene [S1].

### Convex Combination Color Decoder
This variant feeds reflected features $\bar{\mathbf{f}}$ into the color decoder at every sample along the camera ray, rather than just in image space, to aid convergence when geometry is fuzzy [S2]. The final color $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d})$ is computed as a convex combination of view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}_v$ and reflection color $\mathbf{c}_r$:
$$
\mathbf{c} = \beta \mathbf{c}_v + (1 - \beta) \mathbf{c}_r
$$
where $\beta$ is output by geometry encoder followed by sigmoid [S2]. The view-dependent color component $\mathbf{c}_v(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d})$ is computed using MLP $g$ with inputs $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$, bottleneck $\mathbf{b}^{(i)}$, normal $\mathbf{n}^{(i)}$, and direction $\mathbf{d}$: $\mathbf{c}_v = g(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d})$ [S2]. The reflection color component $\mathbf{c}_r(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}')$ is computed using MLP $h$ with inputs $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$, bottleneck $\mathbf{b}^{(i)}$, normal $\mathbf{n}^{(i)}$, dot product $\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)}$, reflected direction $\mathbf{d}'$, and reflection feature $\bar{\mathbf{f}}$: $\mathbf{c}_r = h(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}', \bar{\mathbf{f}})$ [S2].

## Background
The concept of decomposing radiance fields emerged as NeRFs demonstrated strong novel view synthesis capabilities but suffered from shape-radiance ambiguity and poor handling of specularities. Early works like Ref-NeRF [Verbin et al. 2022] introduced normal-based [reparameterization](#11557-reparameterization.md) to model reflections explicitly. Subsequent works such as DE-NeRF [25] and NeRFLight [27] explored explicit separation of geometry (SDFs) and material properties (albedo, roughness) to enable relighting. The use of spherical harmonics for view-dependent features (Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning) addresses the ambiguity by providing a continuous, differentiable basis for angular variation. Recent approaches like NeRF-Casting [S2] refine this by applying reflection features volumetrically to stabilize training.
